title: The Naradasmriti — the Sanskrit text
textType: Law book in verse and prose
author: narada
attributionNote: The law book ascribed to the divine sage Nārada, the messenger of the gods; in its own frame the sages ask Nārada what procedure the courts followed before men fell away from dharma. GRETIL's e-text follows Richard W. Lariviere's critical edition (Philadelphia 1989, University of Pennsylvania Studies on South Asia 4–5) and was input by Yasuke Iriki.
description: The Nāradasmṛti is the procedural law book of classical India: its mātṛkā on the grounds of a lawsuit and the conduct of the parties, its eighteen titles of law treating debt, deposits, partnership, sale without ownership, boundaries, marriage and the marital offences, inheritance, robbery, defamation, assault and gambling, and its appendix on documents — with the rules of pleading, of witnesses and of ordeals that made it the authority on procedure rather than on substantive law.
historicalContext: Composed after the Manusmṛti and cited by every legal digest from the medieval period onward, the text was central to the Anglo-Indian reconstruction of Hindu law: Lariviere's edition and translation replaced the older ones, and the vyavahāra chapters are the fullest statement of Indian civil procedure to survive.
availabilityNote: Complete as GRETIL publishes it: the mātṛkā, the eighteen vyavahārapadas and the pariśiṣṭa, 1,530 verses in all, streamed from GRETIL at read time. The file numbers the work inside its three parts — m for the mātṛkā, v for the vyavahārapada, p for the pariśiṣṭa — and the reader keeps those letters, naming each chapter with the part it belongs to. This is the original Sanskrit, not a translation.
